analysis.title: King dollar's hidden weakness
key_insights: The dollar has resisted bearish narratives and the latest squeeze caught bears off guard, with little meaningful resistance until the 105 level (DXY).
JPM: US yield spreads versus other developed markets are at their widest in 15 months, while the dollar has not kept pace. JPM sees room for the dollar to catch up to rates.
JPM: USD sensitivity to Fed expectations has become much greater than its sensitivity to oil. Oil has been falling without hurting the dollar, so a more hawkish Fed pricing supports it.

JPM: the US yield curve is bear flattening (short-term yields rising on pricing of more Fed tightening). JPM notes this has historically been one of the best environments for the dollar, and is the opposite of the setup that hurt the USD last year.

JPM: SEK is the most vulnerable currency to higher US yields, with USD/SEK rising about 6.3% per 100bps rise in US two-year yields, based on the past year's relationship. JPM prefers SEK as a funding currency.

JPM: yen shorts are complicated by intervention risk. USD/JPY is near 160 while JPM's rate-based model puts fair value near 148, about 11 yen below spot. The gap has persisted since Japan's political shift in October 2025, with policy concerns adding a risk premium to the yen. Intervention risk makes chasing USD/JPY higher look poor on risk/reward.

Deutsche Bank (Mallika Sachdeva): Asia's chip exports generate large surpluses that, unlike petrodollars, are not recycled into US Treasuries but flow into US equities. Foreign equity inflows now exceed $1 trillion annually, with Asia driving much of the recent increase, making the AI boom a key source of US deficit financing.

Deutsche Bank: equity inflows support the dollar and also finance the companies driving the AI buildout, creating a potentially fragile feedback loop. US equities are three times as volatile as Treasuries and tech stocks can be up to ten times as volatile. An unwind of the AI trade could expose the fragility of this funding.
